newsitem.title: POLAND: No proof communists caused Polish pogrom - minister.
newsitem.headline: No proof communists caused Polish pogrom - minister.

text.p: An investigation into the murderous 1946 pogrom in the south Poland town of Kielce has found no reason to suppose it was staged by the then communist authorities, Poland's justice minister said on Thursday.
But minister Leszek Kubicki told a news conference that many circumstances of the pogrom remained unclear after the probe, which was now ending, PAP news agency reported.

Polish leaders voiced shame last July at a ceremony in Kielce over the mob massacre of 42 Jews, who had survived the murder of most of the country's 3.5 million Jews by Nazi German invaders during World War Two.

Since the 1989 fall of communism, Poland's democratic authorities have been trying to find out what lay behind it and since 1992 an official committee for investigating crimes against the Polish nation has been gathering evidence.

Some historians suggest the mob may have been provoked by communist or Soviet agents to reduce support for Poland as it fell under the domination of Moscow and its collaborators, or to discredit domestic opponents of this takeover.
PAP reported Kubicki as saying that, from preliminary information, "the results of the investigation do not provide grounds for hypotheses about a provocation by the authorities."
He said four former members of the old Communist UB security police might face prosecution for having failed to react as they should have done during the pogrom.
The July 4 Kielce pogrom was the worst in a spate of post-war attacks which left about 1,000 Jews dead, promoted a mass exodus of others and entrenched a stereotype of Poles as anti-Semites.
A crowd, enraged by bizarre rumours that Jews had kidnapped a Christian boy for his blood, besieged a three-storey building at 7 Planty Street housing Jewish groups.

Soldiers entered and forced the Jews outside, where a mob of men and women battered them with stones and iron bars. The killings, also of women and children, stretched over many hours while security forces nearby did nothing to help.
Nine Poles were hastily executed after a secretive trial soon afterwards, but the verdicts have been widely questioned.
Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, who apologised for the pogrom in Kielce last year, was in Israel on Thursday in the first visit by a Polish prime minister to the Jewish state.

Part of his aim has been to help dispel mutual prejudices and promote recent efforts to create new relations between Poland and Jewish communities worldwide -- based on the centuries when many Jews found a haven in Poland from persecution elsewhere in Europe.
